1.o: This evangelist begins with the account of Christ's parentage and birth, the ancestors from whom he descended, and the manner of his entry into the world, to make it appear that he was indeed the Messiah promised, for it was foretold that he should be the son of David, and should be born of a virgin; and that he was so is here plainly shown; for here is, I. His pedigree from Abraham in forty-two generations, three fourteens, ver. 1-17. II.
1.i: Matthew 1 opens the New Testament with a genealogy and a quiet moment: a carpenter who decides to trust a dream.
1.p: Lord, You save Your people from their sins. Thank You for Jesus, and for Joseph, who listened and obeyed. Amen.
1.l: Obey something small that you know is right today, even if it is not easy.
q: A genealogy was given to show a promise being kept. What promise in your family has been quietly kept across generations?

2.o: In this chapter, we have the history of our Saviour's infancy, where we find how early he began to suffer, and that in him the word of righteousness was fulfilled, before he himself began to fulfil all righteousness. Here is, I. The wise men's solicitous enquiry after Christ, ver. 1-8. II. Their devout attendance on him, when they found out where he was, ver. 9-12. III. Christ's flight into Egypt, to avoid the cruelty of Herod, ver. 13-15. IV. The barbarous murder of the infants of Bethlehem, ver. 16-18. V.
2.i: Magi from the East follow a star to Jerusalem and Bethlehem, where they worship the child and offer gifts.
2.p: Lord Jesus, You are the King of all nations. Lead us to You, as You led the Magi, and help us to bring our best. Amen.
2.l: Give a gift to Jesus today by doing a kind thing for someone, and tell Him it's for Him.
q: Strangers came a long way to worship the King, while Herod's scholars stayed at home. Who is searching for Jesus today?

3.o: At the start of this chapter, concerning the baptism of John, begins the gospel (Mark i. 1); what went before is but preface or introduction; this is "the beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ." And Peter observes the same date, Acts i. 22, beginning from the baptism of John, for then Christ began first to appear in him, and then to appear to him, and by him to the world. Here is, I. The glorious rising of the morning-star—John the Baptist, ver. 1. 1. The doctrine he preached, ver. 2. 2.
3.i: Jesus is baptized in the Jordan by John, the Spirit descends like a dove, and the Father speaks from heaven.
3.p: Father, You said You loved Your Son. Thank You that You love us too, in Him. Amen.
3.l: Remember today that God loves you, before you do anything, and thank Him for it.
q: The Father said He was pleased with Jesus before Jesus did His work. How does this help you feel loved?

4.o: John Baptist said concerning Christ, He must increase, but I must decrease; and so it proved. For, after John had baptized Christ, and borne his testimony to him, we hear little more of his ministry; he had done what he came to do, and thenceforward there is as much talk of Jesus as ever there had been of John. As the rising Sun advances, the morning star disappears. Concerning Jesus Christ we have in this chapter, I.
4.i: Jesus is tempted by the devil in the wilderness three times, and answers each with Scripture.
4.p: Lord Jesus, You were tested as we are. Help us to know Your word and to use it when we are tempted. Amen.
4.l: Learn one verse from the Bible by heart this week, to use when you are tempted.
q: Jesus answered each test with a verse from the Bible. Which verse would help you the most?

5.o: This chapter, and the two that follow it, are a sermon; a famous sermon; the sermon upon the mount. It is the longest and fullest continued discourse of our Saviour that we have upon record in all the gospels. It is a practical discourse; there is not much of the credenda of Christianity in it—the things to be believed, but it is wholly taken up with the agenda—the things to be done; these Christ began with in his preaching; for if any man will do his will, he shall know of the doctrine, whether it be of God.
5.i: On the mountainside, Jesus gives the Beatitudes and calls his followers salt and light.
5.p: Lord Jesus, make us blessed, salty, and bright. Let others see You in our lives. Amen.
5.l: Do one good thing today where others can see it, and let God have the credit.
q: Jesus called His followers salt and light. Where could you add flavor or light today?

6.o: Christ having, in the former chapter, armed his disciples against the corrupt doctrines and opinions of the scribes and Pharisees, especially in their expositions of the law (that was called their leaven, ch. xvi. 12), comes in this chapter to warn them against their corrupt practices, against the two sins which, though in their doctrine they did not justify, yet in their conversation they were notoriously guilty of, and so as even to recommend them to their admirers: these were hypocrisy and worldly-mindedness…
6.i: Jesus teaches that prayer is for God, not for show, and gives a model prayer that begins, Our Father.
6.p: Our Father in heaven, we love You. Teach us to pray, to forgive, and to trust You for what we need. Amen.
6.l: Find a quiet place today, close the door, and talk to your Father in your own words.
q: Jesus said to pray to your Father in secret. When and where do you pray?

7.o: This chapter continues and concludes Christ's sermon on the mount, which is purely practical, directing us to order our conversation aright, both toward God and man; for the design of the Christian religion is to make men good, every way good. We have, I. Some rules concerning censure and reproof, ver. 1-6. II. Encouragements given us to pray to God for what we need, ver. 7-11. III. The necessity of strictness in conversation urged upon us, ver. 12-14. IV. A caution given us to take heed of false prophets, ver.
7.i: Matthew 7 ends the Sermon on the Mount with a short parable about two houses, and one question: what do you do with what you hear?
7.p: Lord Jesus, You are the rock. Help us not only to hear Your words but to do them, so that we stand when the storms come. Amen.
7.l: Pick one thing Jesus taught that you know, and do it today instead of only thinking about it.
q: What is one thing Jesus has said that you have heard many times but not yet done?

8.o: The evangelist having, in the foregoing chapters, given us a specimen of our Lord's preaching, proceeds now to give some instances of the miracles he wrought, which prove him a Teacher come from God, and the great Healer of a diseased world. In this chapter we have, I. Christ's cleansing of a leper, ver. 1-4. II. His curing a palsy and fever, ver. 5-18. III. His communing with two that were disposed to follow him, ver. 19-22. IV. His controlling the tempest, ver. 23-27. V. His casting out devils, ver. 28-34.
8.s: A Word and It Is Done
8.i: Matthew 8 shows Jesus healing with a touch, healing with a word from far away, and calming a storm with a word.
8.p: Lord Jesus, You speak and it is done. Teach us to trust Your word in the sickroom and in the storm. Amen.
8.l: When something worries you today, tell Jesus about it out loud, ask Him to help, and then wait quietly.
q: What would you ask for if you trusted that a word from him was enough?

9.o: We have in this chapter remarkable instances of the power and pity of the Lord Jesus, sufficient to convince us that he is both able to save to the uttermost all that come to God by him, and as willing as he is able. His power and pity appear here in the good offices he did, I. To the bodies of people, in curing the palsy (ver. 2-8); raising to life the ruler's daughter, and healing the bloody issue (ver. 18-26); giving sight to two blind men (ver. 27-31); casting the devil out of one possessed (ver.
9.i: Matthew 9 tells how a tax collector became a disciple, and why Jesus kept eating with the people others avoided.
9.p: Lord Jesus, You call people who know they need You. Call us, and give us the courage to get up and follow. Amen.
9.l: Invite someone who is left out to sit with you today, at lunch or in a game.
q: What is Jesus asking you to leave behind, or to begin, today?

10.o: This chapter is an ordination sermon, which our Lord Jesus preached, when he advanced his twelve disciples to the degree and dignity of apostles. In the close of the foregoing chapter, he had stirred up them and others to pray that God would send forth labourers, and here we have an immediate answer to that prayer: while they are yet speaking he hears and performs. What we pray for, according to Christ's direction, shall be given, Now here we have, I. The general commission that was given them, ver. 1. II.
10.i: Matthew 10 is Jesus' short training for twelve ordinary men: what to carry, what to say, and what not to fear.
10.p: Father, You count the sparrows and the hairs on our heads. Take our fear away and send us out with Your peace. Amen.
10.l: Give someone a cup of cold water today, or do some other small kindness, because you follow Jesus.
q: The sandal was so cheap and common it was proverbial. What ordinary thing could you set down for a day to travel lighter?

11.o: In this chapter we have, I. The constant and unwearied diligence of our Lord Jesus in his great work of preaching the gospel, ver. 1. II. His discourse with the disciples of John concerning his being the Messiah, ver. 2-6. III. The honourable testimony that Christ bore to John Baptist, ver. 7-15. IV. The sad account he gives of that generation in general, and of some particular places with reference to the success, both of John's ministry and of his own, ver. 16-24. V.
11.s: Come to Me, All You Who Are Weary
11.i: Jesus thanked His Father for revealing truth to the humble, then invited the tired and burdened to come to Him and take His easy yoke.
11.p: Lord Jesus, we come to You tired and burdened. Give us rest, and teach us to walk with You. Amen.
11.l: If you are carrying something heavy today, a worry or a hard job, tell Jesus about it before you tell anyone else.
q: Jesus offers to share the yoke. What are you carrying alone that He could help you pull?

12.o: In this chapter, we have, I. Christ's clearing of the law of the fourth commandment concerning the sabbath-day, and vindicating it from some superstitious notions advanced by the Jewish teachers; showing that works of necessity and mercy are to be done on that day, ver. 1-13. II. The prudence, humility, and self-denial of our Lord Jesus in working his miracles, ver. 14-21. III.
12.i: Matthew 12 is a chapter of arguments over the Sabbath, with Jesus choosing mercy each time.
12.p: Lord of the Sabbath, You give rest and healing together. Teach us to love mercy more than we love being right. Amen.
12.l: Do something kind today instead of only keeping a rule, and ask yourself why the rule was made.
q: The Pharisees knew the rule and missed the mercy. When have you done the same?

13.o: In this chapter, we have, I. The favour which Christ did to his countrymen in preaching the kingdom of heaven to them, ver. 1-2. He preached to them in parables, and here gives the reason why he chose that way of instructing, ver. 10-17. And the evangelist gives another reason, ver. 34, 35. There are eight parables recorded in this chapter, which are designed to represent the kingdom of heaven, the method of planting the gospel kingdom in the world, and of its growth and success.
13.s: A farmer went out to sow his seed
13.i: The sower carried his seed in a basket in his left hand and scattered it with his right, and sowing ran from October to the end of February.
13.l: Notice one ordinary thing today, like a seed or a loaf, and think about what it teaches.
q: Christ taught where all persons might come to him with freedom. Where do you make room for the people nobody makes room for?

14.o: John the Baptist had said concerning Christ, He must increase, but I must decrease, John iii. 30. The morning-star is here disappearing, and the Sun of righteousness rising to its meridian lustre. Here is, I. The martyrdom of John; his imprisonment for his faithfulness to Herod (ver. 1-5), and the beheading of him to please Herodias, ver. 6-12. II. The miracles of Christ. 1. His feeding five thousand men that came to him to be taught, with five loaves and two fishes, ver. 13-21. 2.
14.i: Jesus walked to His friends across a stormy lake, invited Peter to walk to Him, and rescued him when he began to sink, and the disciples worshiped Him.
14.p: Lord Jesus, when we sink, catch us. Teach us to keep our eyes on You, and to worship You as the Son of God. Amen.
14.l: When you feel scared today, look at Jesus and say, Lord, help me. He will hear you.
q: Peter walked while he looked at Jesus and sank when he looked at the waves. What are you looking at?

15.o: In this chapter, we have our Lord Jesus, as the great Prophet teaching, as the great Physician healing, and as the great Shepherd of the sheep feeding; as the Father of spirits instructing them; as the Conqueror of Satan dispossessing him; and as concerned for the bodies of his people, providing for them. Here is, I. Christ's discourse with the scribes and Pharisees about human traditions and injunctions, ver. 1-9. II.
15.s: The Woman Who Would Not Stop Asking
15.i: Matthew 15 starts with an argument about hand-washing and ends with a feast, and between them a woman outside Israel shows what faith looks like.
15.p: Lord, You hear the ones who keep on asking. Give us faith that does not quit, and bread for all who are hungry. Amen.
15.l: When you pray for someone, do not give up after one try. Keep asking, and trust God to hear.
q: 'Dog' could be an insult or a word of humility, depending on who said it. When has the same words meant something different in different mouths?

16.o: None of Christ's miracles are recorded in this chapter, but four of his discourses. Here is, I. A conference with the Pharisees, who challenged him to show them a sign from heaven, ver. 1-4. II. Another with his disciples about the leaven of the Pharisees, ver. 5-12. III. Another with them concerning himself, as the Christ, and concerning his church built upon him, ver. 13-20. IV. Another concerning his sufferings for them, and theirs for him, ver. 21-28. And all these are written for our learning.
16.s: Who Do You Say I Am?
16.i: At Caesarea Philippi, Peter confesses that Jesus is the Christ, and Jesus promises to build his church.
16.p: Lord Jesus, You are the Christ, the Son of the living God. Build Your church in us. Amen.
16.l: Answer Jesus's question in your own words today: Who do you say He is?
q: Peter said it first, but every follower must answer. What is your answer?

17.o: In this chapter we have, I. Christ in his pomp and glory transfigured, ver. 1-13. II. Christ in his power and grace, casting the devil out of a child, ver. 14-21. And, III. Christ in his poverty and great humiliation, 1. Foretelling his own sufferings, ver. 22, 23. 2. Paying tribute, ver. 24-27. So that here is Christ, the Brightness of his Father's glory, by himself purging our sins, paying our debts, and destroying for us him that had the power of death, that is, the devil.
17.i: Peter, James and John saw Jesus shining with glory beside Moses and Elijah, and heard the Father's voice tell them to listen to Him.
17.p: Father, You told us to listen to Your Son. Quiet our hearts and teach us to hear Him. Amen.
17.l: Take one quiet minute today to listen. Turn off the noise and just say, Jesus, I'm listening.
q: Peter wanted to stay on the mountain; the Father said, listen to Him. What do you need to stop talking long enough to hear?

18.o: The gospels are, in short, a record of what Jesus began both to do and to teach. In the foregoing chapter, we had an account of his doings, in this, of his teachings; probably, not all at the same time, in a continued discourse, but at several times, upon divers occasions, here put together, as near akin. We have here, I. Instructions concerning humility, ver. 1-6. II. Concerning offences in general (ver. 7), particularly offences given, 1. By us to ourselves, ver. 8, 9. 2. By us to others, ver. 10-14. 3.
18.i: Peter asked how often to forgive, Jesus said seventy-seven times, and told of a servant forgiven a huge debt who then refused to forgive a small one.
18.p: Lord, You have forgiven us more than we can ever repay. Teach us to forgive others from the heart. Amen.
18.l: Forgive someone today for something small, and tell them you are letting it go. Mean it.
q: The first servant was forgiven a debt he could never repay. How does that change how you forgive?

19.o: In this chapter, we have, I. Christ changing his quarters, leaving Galilee, and coming into the coasts of Judea, ver. 1, 2. II. His dispute with the Pharisees about divorce, and his discourse with his disciples upon occasion of it, ver. 3-12. III. The kind entertainment he gave to some little children which were brought to him, ver. 13-15. IV. An account of what passed between Christ and a hopeful young gentleman that applied himself to him, ver. 16-22. V.
19.s: Through the Eye of a Needle
19.i: Matthew 19 puts three scenes side by side: children welcomed, a wealthy man walking away, and Peter asking what following Jesus costs.
19.p: Lord, we cannot save ourselves. Do what is impossible for us, and make us glad to follow You. Amen.
19.l: Pick one thing you like that you own, and give it away or share it today.
q: Jesus answered a trap by teaching his friends. When someone tests you, what could you learn or teach instead of defending?

20.o: We have four things in this chapter. I. The parable of the labourers in the vineyard, ver. 1-16. II. A prediction of Christ's approaching sufferings, ver. 17-19. III. The petition of two of the disciples, by their mother, reproved, ver. 20-28. IV. The petition of the two blind men granted, and their eyes opened, ver. 29-34.
20.i: A vineyard owner paid every worker a full day's wage, even those who worked only an hour, and said his generosity was not unfair.
20.p: Lord, You are generous beyond our deserving. Free us from envy, and teach us to rejoice in Your gifts to others. Amen.
20.l: Be glad today when something good happens to someone else, even if you did not get it too.
q: The first workers resented the owner's generosity to the last. When have you resented someone else's blessing?

21.o: The death and resurrection of Jesus Christ are the two main hinges upon which the door of salvation turns. He came into the world on purpose to give his life a ransom; so he had lately said, ch. xx. 28. And therefore the history of his sufferings, even unto death, and his rising again, is more particularly recorded by all the evangelists than any other part of his story; and to that this evangelist now hastens apace. For at this chapter begins that which is called the passion-week.
21.s: The King Comes on a Donkey
21.i: On what we call Palm Sunday, Jesus enters Jerusalem the way the prophet Zechariah said a king of peace would come.
21.p: Lord Jesus, gentle King, ride into our hearts. Let our praise be real, not only loud. Amen.
21.l: Sing or shout one happy song of praise to God today, as loud as the children in the temple.
q: The crowd shouted Hosanna on Sunday. What would it take to keep praising when the mood changes?

22.o: This chapter is a continuation of Christ's discourses in the temple, two or three days before he died. His discourses then are largely recorded, as being of special weight and consequence. In this chapter, we have, I. Instruction given, by the parable of the marriage-supper, concerning the rejection of the Jews, and the calling of the Gentiles (ver. 1-10), and, by the doom of the guest that had not the wedding-garment, the danger of hypocrisy in the profession of Christianity, ver. 11-14. II.
22.i: Matthew 22 opens with a parable of a wedding feast, then moves through three questions the leaders ask Jesus.
22.p: Lord, You invite us all to Your table. Make us glad to come, and ready to bring others with us. Amen.
22.l: Invite someone who is often left out to sit with you at lunch or play with you today.
q: Christ knows how to answer our thoughts, not only our words. What have you been thinking that you have not said aloud to him?

23.o: In the foregoing chapter, we had our Saviour's discourses with the scribes and Pharisees; here we have his discourse concerning them, or rather against them. I. He allows their office, ver. 2, 3. II. He warns his disciples not to imitate their hypocrisy and pride, ver. 4-12. III. He exhibits a charge against them for divers high crimes and misdemeanors, corrupting the law, opposing the gospel, and treacherous dealing both with God and man; and to each article he prefixes a woe, ver. 13-33. IV.
23.i: Matthew 23 is Jesus' sharpest speech, aimed at show-off religion, and it ends with the tenderest picture in the chapter: a hen and her chicks.
23.p: Lord, strip away the show from our faith. Gather us under Your wings and make us clean on the inside. Amen.
23.l: Do one helpful thing today that nobody will see, and do not tell anyone.
q: The Mishnah says graves were whitewashed so no one would stumble on one. What looks tidy in you but needs honest cleaning?

24.o: Christ's preaching was mostly practical; but, in this chapter, we have a prophetical discourse, a prediction of things to come; such however as had a practical tendency, and was intended, not to gratify the curiosity of his disciples, but to guide their consciences and conversations, and it is therefore concluded with a practical application.
24.i: Matthew 24 is Jesus' long talk on the Mount of Olives about what lies ahead and how to wait well.
24.p: Lord, You are coming again, and no one knows when. Keep us faithful, awake, and glad to see You. Amen.
24.l: Do your chores today the way a faithful servant would, as if someone important might walk in at any minute.
q: Two events must not be confused. What have you been sure about the timing of that you really don't know?

25.o: This chapter continues and concludes our Saviour's discourse, which began in the foregoing chapter, concerning his second coming and the end of the world. This was his farewell sermon of caution, as that, John xiv. 15, 16, was of comfort to his disciples; and they had need of both in a world of so much temptation and trouble as this is. The application of that discourse, was, Watch therefore, and be ye also ready.
25.i: Ten bridesmaids waited for a late groom; five were ready with oil and joined the feast, and five were not, and Jesus told His friends to keep watch.
25.p: Lord Jesus, You are coming. Keep us watchful, and make us ready, with hearts full of oil. Amen.
25.l: Do one thing today to be ready for something coming up, like packing a bag, or finishing a job early.
q: All ten fell asleep, but only five were ready. What does being ready look like for you?

26.o: The narrative of the death and sufferings of Christ is more particularly and fully recorded by all the four evangelists than any part of his history; for what should be determine, and desire to know, but Christ, and him crucified? And this chapter begins that memorable narrative.
26.i: In the garden of Gethsemane Jesus told His Father exactly how He felt, asked for another way, and then chose His Father's will.
26.p: Father, when we are afraid and sorrowful, teach us to pray honestly and to trust You, as Jesus did. Amen.
26.l: When you are scared or sad, tell God exactly how you feel, the way Jesus did. Then ask Him to help you trust Him.
q: Jesus prayed the same honest prayer three times. What do you keep bringing to God, and are you willing to say not my will but Yours?

27.o: It is a very affecting story which is recorded in this chapter concerning the sufferings and death of our Lord Jesus. Considering the thing itself, there cannot be a more tragical story told us; common humanity would melt the heart, to find an innocent and excellent person thus misused. But considering the design and fruit of Christ's sufferings, it is gospel, it is good news, that Jesus Christ was thus delivered for our offences; and there is nothing we have more reason to glory in than the cross of Christ.
27.i: Matthew 27 follows Jesus from Pilate's courtyard to the tomb, with a governor who washes his hands and a crowd that chooses Barabbas.
27.p: Lord Jesus, You were given up for us. Thank You for staying on the cross when You could have come down. Amen.
27.l: Say thank you to Jesus today for what He did, and thank someone who has helped carry a heavy load for you.
q: Even Judas became a witness to Christ's innocence. When has an unlikely person's honesty cut through a crowd for you?

28.o: In the foregoing chapters, we saw the Captain of our salvation engaged with the powers of darkness, attacked by them, and vigorously attacking them; victory seemed to hover between the combatants; nay, at length, it inclined to the enemies' side, and our Champion fell before them; behold, God has delivered his strength into captivity, and his glory into the enemies' hand.
28.s: All Authority in Heaven and on Earth
28.i: On a Galilee mountain the risen Jesus told His disciples to make disciples of every nation, baptizing and teaching, with the promise that He would be with them always.
28.p: Lord Jesus, You have all authority and You are with us always. Send us in Your name, and make us faithful. Amen.
28.l: Tell one person today something you have learned about Jesus, or invite them to come with you to church or Sunday school.
q: Jesus began with authority and ended with a promise to be with them. Which of the two do you need more today?
